slides.title: Autumn migrants maintain a southwest flight bearing
body: Eastern North American monarch butterflies, _Danaus plexippus_, migrate toward overwintering sites in central Mexico. Some journeys exceed 3,500 km. A **bearing** is a direction measured around the horizon relative to geographic north.

Mouritsen and Frost recorded autumn migrants in an outdoor flight simulator that permitted turning around a vertical tether. Butterflies maintained southwest headings under a visible sky, with a group mean of 225° when their light schedule matched local time.

Their **sun compass** uses solar direction as an orientation reference. Sustained headings establish directional behavior in this preparation, but the tether prevents actual travel. A southwest bearing alone cannot establish destination recognition, route selection or how an insect corrects displacement during a complete migration.

slides.title: A vertical tether preserves turning without translation
body: The simulator separated heading control from forward travel. A fine wire attached to the dorsal thorax allowed the butterfly to rotate freely, while a cylinder approximately 59 cm wide and 64 cm high restricted its view to the sky above.

Vertical airflow supported flight without supplying a horizontal wind direction. The apparatus sampled heading every 200 ms, preserving sustained orientation and changes in course during an individual trial.

Published **virtual trajectories** were reconstructed from those headings using an assumed flight speed. Their apparent distances are therefore calculated paths, not measured displacement. The original trajectories retain evidence of stable versus variable heading, while the preparation excludes landscape landmarks and limits conclusions about unrestricted flight. These constraints allow solar orientation to be tested under controlled visual access.

slides.title: Rotating the apparatus does not rotate the compass
body: A consistent tethered heading could arise from an unnoticed feature of the simulator rather than a geographic cue. Mouritsen and Frost therefore rotated the entire apparatus and separately rotated its components during directional flight.

Butterflies did not follow the new apparatus orientation. When an individual was manually turned away from its established heading, it could return toward the previous geographic direction. The heading records contained sustained orientation despite the absence of forward movement.

These controls reduce explanations based on a fixed mark, mechanical asymmetry or the tether’s angular position. They do not specify which sky cue is necessary. An intervention that changes internal time while retaining the same external sky can distinguish solar orientation with time compensation from a response determined only by the current sun position.

slides.title: Advancing the clock rotates flight toward the southeast
body: **Time compensation** adjusts compass output as the sun changes its position during the day. A **circadian clock** is an internal timing system with a rhythm close to 24 h; **entrainment** aligns its phase with a recurring environmental cycle.

Migrants experienced a 12-h light:12-h dark cycle advanced by 6 h for at least five days. Tested outdoors under the same actual sky as local-time controls, the advanced group oriented near 136°, toward the southeast, rather than the controls’ 225° southwest.

The approximately 89° counterclockwise change links orientation to internal time. An insect treating the afternoon sun as a later time must select a different bearing to maintain its programmed compass relationship. The manipulation supports a time-compensated sun compass, without identifying the clock tissue or its neural output.

slides.title: Delaying the clock produces the opposite heading change
body: A reciprocal clock manipulation tests whether the heading change has the direction expected from solar time compensation. Mouritsen and Frost delayed the entraining 12-h light:12-h dark cycle by 6 h before testing autumn migrants in the same simulator.

Delayed butterflies oriented near 335°, toward the northwest. Relative to the local-time mean of 225°, their heading changed approximately 110° clockwise, opposite to the counterclockwise change after a 6-h advance.

The two shifts support a signed relationship between clock phase and compass direction rather than a nonspecific disturbance from laboratory housing. Their unequal magnitudes reflect the observed solar geometry and experimental conditions. These results establish a compass response to manipulated time, rather than a direct measure of the complete molecular clock or a geographic map.

slides.title: Constant light leaves orientation tied to the visible sun
body: Froy and colleagues compared migrants entrained to local or 6-h-advanced light schedules. Under normal light–dark conditions, their mean headings were 233° and 118°, respectively, retaining the expected dependence on internal time.

After five days in **constant light**, uninterrupted illumination rather than a daily light–dark cycle, the two groups no longer retained their distinct compass bearings. They oriented near 161° while the sun lay approximately between 136° and 160°.

A direction toward the current sun is compatible with **positive phototaxis**, movement toward a light source. Such orientation differs from maintaining a migration bearing as the sun moves. Constant light disrupts normal circadian organization, but it can affect other physiological processes; the treatment does not selectively isolate one clock molecule.

slides.title: Blocking ultraviolet light disrupts sustained flight
body: **Ultraviolet light**, or UV, has shorter wavelengths than human-visible violet light. Froy and colleagues placed a filter blocking wavelengths below 394 nm over outdoor flight tests while retaining approximately 87% of photopic luminous transmission.

The filter interrupted sustained flight or altered heading records; removing it restored sustained flight in most affected butterflies. Sauman and colleagues localized UV-sensitive visual pigment to the **dorsal rim area**, a specialized strip along the upper compound-eye margin.

The reversible effect associates the available UV signal with flight under these conditions. It does not uniquely establish a polarization compass, because the intervention changes spectral input and the continuity of flight together. A loss of stable heading may result partly from altered flight behavior rather than selective removal of directional information.

slides.title: Visible light can entrain the emergence rhythm
body: The wavelengths needed for an oriented-flight assay need not be identical to those that entrain the clock. Froy and colleagues reared pupae under light–dark cycles with a UV-blocking filter and measured the timing of **eclosion**, adult emergence from the pupal case.

Emergence remained concentrated at a particular phase of the daily cycle. Advancing the UV-filtered light schedule by 6 h moved the emergence peaks approximately 5.5 h apart, establishing effective temporal entrainment without ultraviolet illumination.

The result separates a timing response from the previously observed flight disruption. Visible wavelengths can convey daily timing information in this preparation. Eclosion is an output of circadian organization, however, and its entrainment does not by itself identify the sensory pathway that supports migratory heading in an adult.

slides.title: Retinal cells express distinct visual-pigment proteins
body: A compound eye contains repeated optical units called **ommatidia**. Each monarch ommatidium contains photoreceptor cells whose light-sensitive membrane forms a **rhabdom**. An **opsin** is the protein component of a visual pigment that contributes to its spectral sensitivity.

Sauman and colleagues used **in situ hybridization**, labeled probes that locate specific RNA sequences in tissue sections, to identify UV-, blue- and long-wavelength opsin expression. UV and blue opsin RNA occupied R1 or R2 cells; long-wavelength opsin RNA occupied R3–R8.

These distributions establish distinct molecular receptor types in the main retina. They support multiple spectral inputs to vision, but RNA localization alone does not measure a cell’s electrical response or the sensitivity of an entire compass neuron. The reported patterns do not identify downstream transmitters, ion channels or synaptic connections.

slides.title: The dorsal rim area is specialized for ultraviolet input
body: The dorsal rim area differs molecularly from adjacent main-retina ommatidia. Sauman and colleagues found UV opsin RNA throughout R1–R8 in this strip, with no detected blue or long-wavelength opsin RNA in those dorsal-rim cells.

The specialization extended approximately 40–50 ommatidia along the eye margin and one to three ommatidia inward, totaling roughly 100 per eye. Antibody labeling localized UV opsin protein to their rhabdoms; adjacent retinal tissue provided a comparison with mixed receptor types.

A common spectral class is consistent with sampling polarization without mixing distinct color signals. **Linear polarization** specifies the orientation of the light wave’s electric field. Molecular specialization supports a candidate polarization input, but selective expression alone does not establish how the animal uses that input during migration.

slides.title: Polarizer rotation changes flight in a restricted assay
body: Sauman and colleagues tested tethered monarchs beneath a linear polarizing filter that restricted skylight access to an 80° field and excluded direct sight of the sun. Turning the filter by 90° changed the available electric-field orientation.

Sequential 5-min records compared flight before rotation, after rotation, during UV interference below 397 nm, and after removing the UV filter. UV interference often produced circling and reduced virtual progress by at least 70%; removal restored sustained directional flight.

The responses support sensitivity to manipulated polarized UV under this restricted arrangement. They do not establish that natural migration depends on the same cue. Spectral interference also altered flight continuity, and a polarizer can introduce brightness-dependent effects that require separate controls. The UV-specialized dorsal rim provides an anatomical candidate for this input.

slides.title: Polarized-light behavior requires brightness controls
body: Stalleicken and colleagues compared orientation under a polarizing filter when the sun was excluded, when the sun was visible, and with an unpolarized-light control. Their controlled tests did not establish reliable migratory orientation based on polarized skylight alone.

With the sun available, monarchs retained directional orientation. The study identified brightness-related cues associated with the experimental optical arrangement as a possible contributor to earlier polarizer responses; rotating a filter need not change only polarization direction.

These findings qualify the behavioral interpretation without denying polarization-sensitive visual physiology. A response to an artificial stimulus and a cue’s necessity for migration are different claims. Natural compass use requires controls that separate polarization from intensity patterns and access to other celestial cues, rather than treating every polarizer-induced turn as time-compensated navigation.

slides.title: Dorsal-rim masking leaves sun-based orientation intact
body: Selective masking asks whether the UV-specialized dorsal eye margin is necessary when other sky cues remain available. Stalleicken and colleagues covered the dorsal rim area and compared migratory orientation with that of untreated butterflies under a visible sun.

Masked animals retained directional flight, and the study’s clock-shifted tests remained consistent with a time-compensated sun compass. The published eye preparation documents the position of the mask rather than assuming that the whole retina was obstructed.

The result supports a sun-based pathway that can operate without normal dorsal-rim input in these conditions. It does not establish that polarization information is never used or that every possible sky condition yields the same outcome. Receptor specialization, neural responsiveness and behavioral necessity must be tested separately.

slides.title: Emergence persists without a daily light signal
body: An endogenous rhythm continues after the external cycle is removed. Froy and colleagues entrained monarch pupae under a light–dark schedule and then compared adult emergence in continued cycling light, constant darkness and constant light.

Eclosion clustered early in the light phase and remained rhythmic in constant darkness. A 6-h shift in the prior light schedule altered the emergence phase. Constant light disrupted the normal temporal concentration of emergence.

Persistence in darkness supports an internal circadian oscillator rather than an immediate response only to lights turning on. **Free-running** means that a rhythm proceeds without daily entrainment. The emergence assay establishes an endogenous timing output, but its phase and tissue requirements should not automatically be equated with the adult migratory compass.

slides.title: The per transcript changes with circadian phase
body: The **period gene**, abbreviated _per_, encodes a clock-associated protein. Froy and colleagues measured its RNA in monarch heads across the day to connect behavioral timing with a molecular rhythm. **Transcription** is the production of RNA from a DNA template.

Head _per_ RNA was higher at night and lower during the day in a light–dark cycle. Its rhythm persisted, with altered amplitude and phase, in constant darkness; constant light maintained comparatively low, nonrhythmic levels in this assay.

The molecular and emergence measurements support endogenous circadian organization. Whole-head sampling combines multiple tissues, however, so the RNA profile does not locate a unique compass clock. A rhythmic transcript is a candidate component whose functional role requires perturbation, rather than proof that its abundance alone specifies flight direction.

slides.title: CRY2 represses clock-controlled transcription
body: **CRY2** is the second monarch cryptochrome and has a different tested role from CRY1. Zhu and colleagues introduced clock proteins into DpN1 cells and measured a _per_ regulatory sequence coupled to a **luciferase reporter**, a light-producing readout of transcriptional activity.

slides.title: Reducing CRY2 removes normal transcriptional repression
body: A loss-of-function test complements adding CRY2 to a transcriptional reporter. Zhu and colleagues reduced endogenous CRY2 in DpN1 cells using RNA interference and compared the treatment with interference directed against a control sequence.

slides.title: Clock proteins form complexes that support CRY2 stability
body: Clock regulation depends on protein interactions as well as transcription. Zhu and colleagues used **co-immunoprecipitation**, antibody capture of a protein together with associated molecules, to examine PER, TIM and CRY2 in monarch brain extracts and cultured cells.

slides.title: Removing antennae disrupts the group compass bearing
body: The **antennae** are paired head appendages that contain sensory tissue and molecular clocks. Merlin and colleagues removed the antennal flagella, the long distal portions, and compared migratory orientation with intact butterflies.

Intact animals oriented near 211° on the normal light schedule and near 355° after a 6-h delay. Antenna-less butterflies could sustain an individual heading, but their directions no longer formed the normal common migratory bearing across animals.

The dissociation identifies an antennal contribution to time-compensated orientation rather than a complete loss of flight or direction-holding ability. Removal affects several antennal functions, so this experiment alone cannot assign the deficit specifically to a molecular clock. Paint and isolated-tissue experiments test the timing explanation more selectively.

slides.title: Antenna-less butterflies remain capable of free flight
body: An orientation deficit requires a motor control when the manipulated organ could influence flight. Merlin and colleagues released intact and antenna-less monarchs outdoors and compared whether they could maintain normal upward flight.

Most butterflies in both conditions flew normally after release. In simulator trials, antenna-less individuals also retained directional flight within a recording, despite losing the consistent group bearing expected from the entraining light cycle.

The combined observations reduce an explanation based on general inability to fly. They do not prove that antennal removal leaves every aspect of aerodynamic control unchanged. The measured outcome is sufficient to separate severe flight incapacity from compass disorganization, while preserving the need to identify which antennal signal supports the shared migratory direction.

slides.title: One functioning antenna is sufficient for compensation
body: Guerra and colleagues tested migrants after removing either the left or the right antenna. The remaining appendage retained access to light, allowing its timing contribution to be evaluated without a second functional antenna.

The results support functional sufficiency of either antenna under the tested conditions. They do not establish how outputs from two intact antennae are combined. A system can work with one source of timing yet become disrupted when a second source supplies a conflicting signal rather than no signal.

slides.title: Conflicting antennal timing disrupts the shared bearing
body: Guerra and colleagues painted one antenna black and the other clear, leaving one light-accessible timing system alongside one deprived of normal photic entrainment. They compared the condition with the orientation supported by a single accessible antenna.

slides.title: Removing the conflicting antenna restores orientation
body: A within-animal rescue tested whether the abnormal second antenna caused the compass deficit. Guerra and colleagues first flew migrants with one black-painted and one clear-painted antenna, then removed the black-painted appendage and tested flight again.

Combining repeated-flight and first-flight removal controls gave a mean near 216°, reducing an explanation based on experience with the simulator alone. The clear antenna remained available throughout the intervention.

It supports coordinated antennal timing input while leaving its neural integration mechanism unidentified. The rescue does not imply that antennal removal is generally beneficial; its effect depends on which timing source is removed.

slides.title: Central-complex neuropils define a compass substrate
body: Heinze and Reppert mapped the monarch **central complex** using synapsin antibody labeling and three-dimensional reconstruction. The central body has upper and lower divisions, associated with a **protocerebral bridge**, a transverse neuropil, and paired **noduli**, compact neighboring neuropils.

The **anterior optic tubercle** is an additional visual-processing region. The **lateral accessory lobe** lies beside the central complex and receives identified neuronal processes associated with compass circuitry. Source scale bars distinguish whole-brain organization at 500 µm from central-complex details at 50 µm.

This anatomy specifies locations for cell recording and dye reconstruction. Synapse-rich boundaries do not themselves identify information flow, transmitter identity or behavioral necessity. Combining the map with individual-cell physiology tests which neurons respond to skylight cues rather than assigning a compass function from location alone.

slides.title: Dye-filled neurons connect visual input to compass regions
body: Heinze and Reppert combined intracellular recordings with dye injection to recover the anatomy of individual compass-related neurons. **Intracellular recording** measures electrical activity from within a cell; subsequent dye filling associates that response with its neuronal processes.

Tangential neurons TL2 and TL3 connected the **lateral triangle**, an input region near the lateral accessory lobe, with distinct layers of the lower central body. Their processes spread across this compass-associated neuropil. The recovered pathways provide candidate stages through which visual information reaches central-complex activity.

The recovered projections and light responses support a circuit-level organization, but morphological polarity does not establish every synaptic connection. The studies did not identify a complete sequence of neurotransmitters, postsynaptic receptors or ion channels through the migratory compass pathway.

slides.title: Compass neurons respond to the polarization axis
body: Heinze and Reppert presented polarized 365-nm UV light from above while recording identified compass neurons. The electric-field orientation, called the **E-vector**, rotated through 360° at controlled speeds of 30° or 60° per second.

**Action potentials**, brief electrical spikes, occurred at different rates for different E-vector angles. Preferred and suppressed axes were approximately 90° apart, and the response repeated after 180°, matching the axial symmetry of linear polarization. Intracellular traces preserved voltage and time calibration.

These measurements establish neuronal sensitivity to polarization under controlled stimulation. They do not prove that this cue is necessary for migratory orientation when the sun is available. Behavioral masking and sensory recordings address different causal claims, even when they concern related input structures.

slides.title: The same compass circuit represents solar azimuth
body: **Azimuth** is the angular position of a stimulus around the horizon. Heinze and Reppert moved an unpolarized light spot around the animal at 30° elevation while recording compass-related cells responsive to skylight polarization.

The cells also changed spike rate with spot azimuth. Tests used UV at 365 nm, blue at 470 nm and green at 530 nm; many cells responded to multiple wavelengths with comparable preferred directions rather than opposite spectral preferences.

These responses support convergence of polarization and sun-like positional signals within the compass network. An isolated spot is a controlled proxy for solar direction, rather than the full natural sky. The experiment identifies neuronal coding of cue position, but not a complete transformation from retinal photoreceptors through named chemical synapses to steering muscles.

slides.title: Dorsal masking separates two converging visual inputs
body: A neuron responsive to both polarization and a light spot could receive those signals through the same receptors or through separate inputs. Heinze and Reppert covered the dorsal visual field and repeated both stimulus tests during intracellular recording.

slides.title: Migratory butterflies have narrower green-light tuning
body: Nguyen and colleagues compared tangential-neuron recordings from autumn migrants with non-migratory monarchs. They rotated a green 530-nm light spot at 30° elevation and measured the angular range producing elevated spike rates.

**Full width at half maximum** measures a tuning curve’s width at half its peak response. Mean green-light width was approximately 83° in migrants and 118° in non-migrants. Peak rates were broadly similar, so the distinction concerned angular selectivity more than a simple increase in firing.

The comparison associates migratory condition with narrower solar-proxy tuning. Wild migrants and commercially sourced non-migrants differed in origin and rearing, however, so migration state was not isolated experimentally. The measurements do not establish that narrower tuning causes improved migratory accuracy.

slides.title: Migratory tuning concentrates sensitivity near the front
body: Nguyen and colleagues analyzed how strongly a change in green-light azimuth altered tangential-neuron activity. This **angular sensitivity** depends on the slope of the tuning response, rather than its maximum firing rate alone.

Migrant recordings concentrated greater sensitivity within approximately 60° of the preferred direction. Non-migrant responses distributed more sensitivity along flanks roughly 60°–180° away. The published analysis used 5° angular bins and compared the pattern with solar geometry expected during migration.

The pattern supports a physiological difference in how nearby directions are discriminated. Its proposed relevance to frontal sun positions is an interpretation based on cue geometry. The study did not manipulate tuning width during free migration or establish a causal gain in arrival accuracy; cohort origin and rearing remained potential confounds.

slides.title: Spring remigrants reverse direction but retain compensation

The comparison supports a change in the selected migratory direction while preserving the timing-based orientation mechanism. A **disappearance bearing** is the final observed direction after release, rather than a complete travel route. Seasonal reversal does not establish a different clock tissue or reveal how the preferred direction is represented in the nervous system.

body: Guerra and Reppert exposed fall migrants to 24 days resembling the overwintering thermal environment: 11°C during the light phase and 4°C during darkness. One treatment gradually increased day length; another maintained a constant 12-h light:12-h dark cycle.

Northward orientation therefore did not require the treatment’s changing photoperiod, the daily duration of light.

The 24-day treatment establishes an effective exposure, rather than the minimum cold duration required for reversal.

slides.title: Goal coding differs from coding the current heading
body: Beetz and colleagues recorded central-complex neurons while non-migratory monarchs oriented toward a virtual sun. A **heading signal** represents current orientation; a **goal-direction signal** represents the direction the animal attempts to maintain.

Moving the sun-like stimulus altered heading-related tuning, while candidate goal cells retained their association with the chosen target. Aversive conditioning using neck stimulation changed the selected goal by about 130° on average; goal-related neural tuning changed with that preference rather than simply following a solar displacement.

items.text: Advancing and delaying the entraining light cycle rotate migratory headings in opposite directions. A compass bearing is distinct from a geographic map or a complete migration route.
Either light-accessible antenna can support compensation. Conflicting antennal timing disrupts the shared bearing, and removing the conflicting antenna restores orientation.
CRY1 supplies light-sensitive clock input, while CRY2 represses clock-controlled transcription. Protein interactions and timed nuclear localization contribute to the feedback cycle.
Central-complex neurons encode polarization and sun-like azimuth. Neural sensitivity to polarization does not establish its necessity for migration when the sun is available.
Effective multiweek cold exposure induces northward orientation while time compensation remains available. Warm aging alone did not produce reversal in the tested migrants.
Current heading and desired direction have distinct neuronal correlates. A complete causal pathway from antennal timing through compass computation to steering remains unidentified.
